Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

issues.item: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other selected items describe fear-based reactivity, hypervigilance, sexual trauma triggers, and intrusive/reliving memory phenomena after rape. In that context, prominent risk-taking pulls in the opposite direction of the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation and is not supported by appraisals or maladaptive-strategy items. This creates a within-node and cross-node coherence problem.

vignette:
Priya is a 61-year-old South Asian woman who immigrated to the Central Valley of California decades ago, where she has spent most of her adult life working the fields alongside her husband. She is soft-spoken and deliberate in her speech, and it took her several sessions before she could describe what happened to her in anything approaching full detail. What she eventually disclosed was this: approximately fourteen months ago, she was working alone at the edge of an irrigation ditch at dusk, waiting for a co-worker who never arrived, when a man she recognized vaguely from a neighboring property attacked her. He came from behind, and the assault happened on the ground, in the dirt, with a farm dog barking somewhere nearby - a sound that continued throughout. She did not scream. She told herself afterward, and then told herself again, that she had simply frozen, though she has spent the months since trying to understand what that means about her.

In the weeks that followed, Priya said very little to anyone. She returned to work because the family needed her income and because stopping felt, in some way she could not articulate, like admitting that something permanent had happened. But the fields had changed. The same low light at the end of a shift, the same smell of turned earth, the same sound of a dog from a neighboring property - any of these could bring the full memory back without the slightest warning, not as a recollection but as an event happening in real time, her body pressed into the ground again, the weight and the sound and the particular quality of the fading sky above her. She described this to her therapist as "the film that plays again," and she said it plays whether she wants it to or not. There is no distance in it. When it comes, she is there.

She had come to believe that her body understood danger in a way her mind no longer trusted. Before she could register that a co-worker had placed a hand on her shoulder to get her attention, she would be on her feet, heart hammering, several steps away. She was certain that something in her had been rewired, that her reactions were no longer under her control, and this frightened her almost as much as the memory itself. At night she lay awake listening - to her husband's breathing, to sounds from the road, to nothing in particular - because sleep felt like a surrender of the only vigilance she had left.

Her marriage had quietly hollowed out over the course of the year. Her husband, a patient and gentle man by her account, had tried more than once to be close to her, and each time she had withdrawn so completely that he had eventually stopped trying. She had not explained why. She did not know how to explain it without explaining everything, and she was not ready for that. What frightened her most about intimacy now was not the act itself but the way it collapsed time - the way closeness could make the memory present again in an instant. The distance between them had grown into something neither of them named, and Priya carried a private grief about this that she had not shared with anyone before coming to therapy.

Dogs remained a particular problem. The agricultural work she depends on puts her in proximity to farm dogs almost daily, and she had begun arriving earlier in the morning and leaving before the neighboring property's dog was let out, rearranging her schedule in ways her employer had noticed and questioned. She had offered vague explanations. The reorganization of her days around a single animal had cost her hours and a degree of professional standing she had built over many years.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was a conversation with her daughter, who lives nearby and had noticed the changes in her mother's face and manner. Her daughter said simply that she was scared for her, and Priya had cried for the first time since the assault. She came to therapy the following week. What she is most hoping for, she said quietly in the first session, is to be able to stand in a field at dusk again without leaving herself.
